current_revisions.prompt: Describe the flame-test colours of lithium and sodium compounds.
current_revisions.answer: Lithium gives a red flame; sodium gives a bright-yellow flame.
credit: Lithium: red flame (1).
Sodium: bright-yellow flame (1).

current_revisions.prompt: Describe two headings, beyond sample identity, needed in a results table for comparing repeated flame tests of lithium samples. The table must distinguish the flame observation from any pre-existing sample colour.
current_revisions.answer: Use a column headed “flame colour”, rather than simply “colour”, and identify each trial or repeat so separate observations are retained.
credit: A clearly labelled flame-colour observation column, distinct from sample colour (1).
A trial/repeat identifier or separate repeat columns, so repeated observations are recorded independently (1).

current_revisions.prompt: Describe the conclusions from three flame-test repeats. Reference sodium colour: bright yellow. Sample P gives yellow, yellow, yellow; sample Q gives red, yellow, red under the same conditions.
current_revisions.answer: P gives a reproducible result consistent with sodium. Q is inconsistent, so its single yellow result is not enough for a dependable identification.
credit: P consistently matches the supplied sodium reference (1).
Q is inconsistent; one yellow trial cannot support a dependable identification (1).

current_revisions.prompt: Describe the contrasting flame colours expected from potassium and barium compounds.
current_revisions.answer: Potassium gives lilac; barium gives green.
credit: Potassium: lilac (1).
Barium: green (1).

current_revisions.prompt: Explain why a yellow flame does not exclude potassium when a sample may also contain sodium. The sodium flame is much brighter than the potassium flame.
current_revisions.answer: The bright sodium emission can dominate the visible colour and mask the weaker lilac potassium flame, so absence of visible lilac is not evidence that potassium is absent.
credit: Brighter sodium colour can mask the weaker potassium colour (1).
Failure to see potassium colour therefore cannot establish absence of potassium (1).

current_revisions.prompt: Describe the flame colour of a calcium compound and state the physical feature being observed in a flame test.
current_revisions.answer: Calcium gives a brick-red flame. It is the flame colour being recorded, not the colour of a solution or precipitate.
credit: Calcium: brick-red (1).
Colour belongs to the flame, rather than a solution or precipitate (1).

current_revisions.prompt: Describe two improvements to this calcium flame-test record before comparing repeat trials: “Test looked red. The room lights were changed between trials.”
current_revisions.answer: Record the precise flame shade, distinguishing brick-red from a general red description, and keep viewing conditions or lighting the same between trials.
credit: Record the actual flame shade precisely rather than the vague word red (1).
Keep illumination/viewing conditions constant for a fair comparison (1).

current_revisions.prompt: Deduce the identification supported by this two-stage result and how it resolves the original uncertainty. A sample first gave an indistinct greenish flame. References: barium sulfate forms an insoluble white precipitate; potassium sulfate remains soluble. Adding dilute sulfate solution to a fresh sample gives a white precipitate.
current_revisions.answer: Barium is supported. The precipitation result distinguishes it from the supplied potassium alternative, whereas the indistinct flame alone did not.
credit: Barium supported by the white sulfate precipitate (1).
The fresh-portion result discriminates from soluble potassium sulfate and resolves the ambiguous flame (1).

current_revisions.prompt: Plan how to arrange a comparison of barium flame-test repeats when one salt is tested as a large wet lump and the other as a small dry sample. Do not infer identity from differences in brightness.
current_revisions.answer: Use small comparable quantities prepared consistently and keep flame position/viewing conditions consistent; compare the characteristic colour rather than brightness alone.
credit: Make sample amount/preparation comparable, avoiding wet-lump versus dry-small-sample differences (1).
Use consistent flame/viewing conditions and compare colour rather than brightness alone (1).

current_revisions.prompt: Describe the chemical test for ammonia gas, including the condition of the indicator paper and its positive change.
current_revisions.answer: Expose damp red litmus paper to the gas; it turns blue.
credit: Damp red litmus paper exposed to the gas (1).
Paper turns blue (1).

current_revisions.prompt: Describe the test for carbon dioxide and its positive observation.
current_revisions.answer: Bubble the gas through fresh limewater; the limewater becomes milky.
credit: Pass the gas through fresh limewater (1).
Limewater becomes milky/cloudy from a white precipitate (1).

current_revisions.prompt: Describe the test for chlorine gas and the final positive observation.
current_revisions.answer: Expose damp litmus paper to the gas; the paper is bleached.
credit: Damp litmus exposed to the gas (1).
Its colour is bleached/removed (1).

current_revisions.prompt: Describe the test for a small separately collected hydrogen sample and the positive observation.
current_revisions.answer: Under teacher supervision, apply a lighted splint to the small collected sample; a squeaky pop is heard.
credit: Lighted splint applied to a small separately collected sample (1).
Squeaky pop (1).

current_revisions.prompt: Describe the test for oxygen and its positive observation.
current_revisions.answer: Insert a glowing splint into the gas; the splint relights.
credit: Glowing, non-flaming splint (1).
Splint relights (1).

current_revisions.prompt: State the structural feature of CH2=CHCH3 responsible for its rapid reaction with bromine water.
credit: The carbon–carbon double bond (1).

current_revisions.prompt: Calculate the delivered volume from burette readings of 1.20 cm³ initially and 24.80 cm³ finally, when both readings are 0.20 cm³ too high.
current_revisions.answer: Corrected readings are 1.00 cm³ and 24.60 cm³. Delivered volume = 24.60 − 1.00 = 23.60 cm³; the equal offsets cancel.
credit: 23.60 cm³; accept subtraction of either the two corrected readings or the two recorded readings, since equal offsets cancel (1).

current_revisions.prompt: State the anion indicated when a sample confirmed free of ammonium gives ammonia on warming with NaOH and aluminium foil.
credit: Nitrate / NO3⁻ (1).

limits: Coverage is a direct text/credit check, not independent certification of every objective or cognitive-demand judgement.
